title: ELEPHANT: Measuring and understanding social sycophancy in LLMs
topic: Social Aspects->Fairness, Equity, Justice and Safety
claim: A multi-part benchmark combines several datasets, human-validated scorers and comparison metrics to measure a multi-dimensional behavior, including consistency across opposing perspectives.
layout: 4 columns, left-to-right, datasets feeding scorers into two outputs, orange highlights
description: A wide, left-to-right block diagram with four rounded gray-blue containers. At the left, a large 'Datasets' box stacks four colored bars: a green OEQ bar for general advice queries, orange AITA-YTA and SS bars, and an AITA-NTA-FLIP group holding an original 'NTA' post (green) and a flipped 'NTA' post (orange). Arrows lead to a middle column. There, 'Prompt LLM' feeds a purple-monospace 'LLM response' with a robot icon. Beside it sits a blue 'crowdsourced response' with a people icon. Both flow into a 'Human-validated sycophancy scorers' box listing Validation, Indirectness and Framing. The right column has two outputs: 'Sycophancy scores', which compares LLM and crowdsourced responses, and 'Moral sycophancy', which compares original and flipped perspectives. A long arrow runs from the NTA-FLIP group through an 's^NTA: YTA vs. NTA' box to the moral output. Orange marks the datasets where affirmation is especially problematic.
caption: Overview of our ELEPHANT benchmark, which measures four dimensions of social sycophancy for a given LLM using four datasets: open-ended advice queries (OEQ) and three datasets where affirmation is particularly problematic (with orange boxes: AITA-YTA, SS, AITA-NTA-FLIP). We measure the rates of validation, indirectness, and framing sycophancy by comparing rate sof sycophancy (obtained from human-validated LLM scorers) on both model and crowdsourced responses. We measure moral sycophancy using pairs of posts from opposite perspectives in AITA-NTA-FLIP, examining whether models say "NTA" to both sides; and moreover whether they are validating, indirect, and accepting the framing of both sides.
abstract: LLMs are known to exhibit sycophancy: agreeing with and flattering users, even at the cost of correctness. Prior work measures sycophancy only as direct agreement with users' explicitly stated beliefs that can be compared to a ground truth. This fails to capture broader forms of sycophancy such as affirming a user's self-image or other implicit beliefs. To address this gap, we introduce social sycophancy, characterizing sycophancy as excessive preservation of a user's face (their desired self-image), and present ELEPHANT, a benchmark for measuring social sycophancy in an LLM. Applying our benchmark to 11 models, we show that LLMs consistently exhibit high rates of social sycophancy: on average, they preserve user's face 45 percentage points more than humans in general advice queries and in queries describing clear user wrongdoing (from Reddit's r/AmITheAsshole). Furthermore, when prompted with perspectives from either side of a moral conflict, LLMs affirm both sides (depending on whichever side the user adopts) in 48% of cases--telling both the at-fault party and the wronged party that they are not wrong--rather than adhering to a consistent moral or value judgment. We further show that social sycophancy is rewarded in preference datasets, and that while existing mitigation strategies for sycophancy are limited in effectiveness, model-based steering shows promise for mitigating these behaviors. Our work provides theoretical grounding and an empirical benchmark for understanding and addressing sycophancy in the open-ended contexts that characterize the vast majority of LLM use cases.
